cases.title: Failure to Thrive in Infancy
cases.stem: An 8-month-old infant, Hannah, is referred for poor weight gain. Her mother says she breastfeeds but the infant tires quickly, feeds for short periods, and often seems irritable afterward. Hannah’s weight is well below the expected curve, and her father says she has fewer wet nappies than her older sibling did at the same age. The nurse notes thin extremities, poor growth compared with previous records, and developmental interaction that seems less energetic than expected. The infant does not appear acutely unstable, but the nurse recognises a concerning long-term pattern.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support failure to thrive? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: Failure to thrive is identified through poor growth plus feeding and hydration concerns. The nurse must recognise both the nutritional and developmental implications.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Growth failure requiring assessment of intake, health status, and caregiver factors
No concern if the infant is quiet

questions.rationale: Poor growth must be evaluated thoroughly. The causes may be nutritional, medical, developmental, or psychosocial.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Inadequate nutrition and hydration affecting growth and development

questions.rationale: The main concern is impaired growth and potentially underlying illness or feeding dysfunction.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Perform detailed nutritional, hydration, and developmental assessment and collaborate for further evaluation
Assume the infant will outgrow the issue without follow-up

questions.rationale: A structured assessment is essential in failure to thrive. Delay risks ongoing harm to growth and development.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Review feeding frequency, duration, and technique
Assess parent understanding and psychosocial stressors respectfully
Watch for medical clues such as vomiting, cardiac strain, or malabsorption signs

questions.rationale: Failure to thrive requires sensitive, nonjudgmental assessment. Causes may be multifactorial and should never be reduced to blame.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement over time?

options.text: Weight gain trend improves, feeding becomes more effective, hydration markers improve, and developmental engagement strengthens
Growth continues to fall with no reassessment

questions.rationale: Improvement is measured through sustained growth, better intake, and improved developmental and hydration status.

cases.title: Croup versus Epiglottitis Recognition
cases.stem: A 3-year-old child, Lucas, is brought to the emergency department with noisy breathing. He has a harsh barking cough and inspiratory stridor. His father says he had a cold yesterday and became much worse tonight. The nurse notices that the child is anxious but can still swallow saliva. In another room, a 4-year-old with sudden high fever, drooling, muffled voice, and tripod positioning is also being assessed. The nurse must distinguish between croup and a more dangerous upper airway emergency such as epiglottitis.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which finding is more suggestive of epiglottitis than croup?

options.text: Drooling with muffled voice and tripod positioning

questions.rationale: Drooling, muffled voice, high fever, and tripod positioning are classic red flags for epiglottitis and indicate a more dangerous airway emergency than typical croup.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Both children can be managed identically
The child with drooling and tripod positioning may have impending airway obstruction and requires higher urgency
Barking cough is always more dangerous than drooling

questions.rationale: The nurse must distinguish between typical croup and epiglottitis-like presentation. Epiglottitis is far more dangerous because agitation or unnecessary examination may worsen obstruction.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent in the child with drooling and tripod positioning?
questions.rationale: Potential airway collapse is the life-threatening issue.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first for suspected epiglottitis?

options.text: Keep the child calm, avoid unnecessary throat examination, and escalate urgently for advanced airway-capable assessment
Force the child to lie flat
Use a tongue depressor to inspect the throat

questions.rationale: Agitation and throat manipulation can worsen obstruction. The nurse should prioritise calm, upright positioning and urgent expert airway support.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Differentiate croup and epiglottitis using airway severity cues
Provide humidified support or ordered therapy for croup while monitoring closely
Involve caregivers in keeping the child calm
Reassess stridor, retractions, and energy level frequently
Assume all stridor is low priority

questions.rationale: Stridor in children is always important. The nurse must tailor care according to likely cause and severity.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement in the child with croup?

options.text: Stridor decreases, work of breathing lessens, and the child appears calmer after treatment
Retractions worsen and the child becomes more fatigued
Monitoring stops when the child becomes quiet without assessment

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in better airway comfort, less distress, and reduced respiratory effort.

cases.title: Fracture with Neurovascular Compromise Risk
cases.stem: A 9-year-old child, Emma, is brought to the emergency department after falling from playground equipment. She has an obvious deformity of the forearm and is crying in pain. Her father says she has not wanted him to touch the arm and keeps saying her fingers feel strange. On assessment, the nurse notes swelling, pain, decreased willingness to move the fingers, and coolness distal to the injury. The child can wiggle the fingers slightly but says they feel numb. The nurse suspects fracture with possible neurovascular compromise risk.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest neurovascular compromise risk? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: All findings are important. Numbness and coolness suggest potential compromise of circulation or nerve function. Severe pain with swelling can also signal compartment concerns.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Fracture with possible neurovascular compromise requiring urgent assessment

questions.rationale: The child’s symptoms point beyond pain alone. Distal changes are especially important in extremity injuries.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for impaired circulation and nerve function distal to the fracture

questions.rationale: Neurovascular compromise can lead to permanent damage if not identified and managed quickly.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Support immobilisation, assess pain and distal circulation/sensation carefully, and prepare for urgent fracture management
Encourage vigorous finger exercise against resistance immediately
Delay assessment because swelling is expected

questions.rationale: Immobilisation and neurovascular assessment are the priorities. Tight wrapping or delayed reassessment may worsen compromise.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess pulses, colour, warmth, movement, and sensation regularly
Explain procedures clearly to child and caregiver
Watch for increasing pain out of proportion to injury
Ignore numbness because fractures are painful

questions.rationale: All these actions are appropriate. Pain out of proportion and numbness may indicate worsening compartment syndrome or neurovascular injury and must not be ignored.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective early management?

options.text: Pain is better controlled, immobilisation is maintained, and distal circulation/sensation remain intact or improve
Fingers become colder and less responsive
Monitoring stops after the first splint is applied

questions.rationale: Effective management protects the limb, controls pain, and preserves neurovascular function.

cases.title: Neonatal or Young Infant Sepsis Presentation
cases.stem: A 3-week-old infant is brought in because the parents say she is not feeding well, seems sleepier than usual, and had a low temperature at home earlier today. The infant looks pale and does not wake vigorously for feeding. The parents say she usually cries strongly, but today she is quiet and difficult to rouse. On assessment, the nurse notes poor feeding, lethargy, mottled skin, and borderline temperature instability. The nurse recognises that very young infants may show infection with subtle but dangerous signs.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are concerning for sepsis in this young infant? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: All these are important warning signs. Neonates and young infants may show infection through poor feeding and subtle behavioural changes rather than dramatic symptoms.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Possible neonatal/young infant sepsis requiring urgent evaluation

questions.rationale: The infant’s combination of poor feeding, lethargy, and mottling should be treated as high-risk until proven otherwise.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for overwhelming infection and impaired perfusion

questions.rationale: Very young infants can deteriorate rapidly. Perfusion, breathing, and infection management are urgent.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Escalate urgently, assess ABCs and perfusion, support temperature management, and prepare for sepsis evaluation and treatment
Delay action because the infant is quiet
Feed and send home without review
Ignore low temperature because fever is absent

questions.rationale: Absence of high fever does not make sepsis unlikely in very young infants. Quietness and poor feeding are not reassuring.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor colour, tone, perfusion, and feeding closely
Communicate clearly with parents while urgent care continues
Prepare for investigations and antimicrobial therapy as ordered
Assume a sleeping infant is always stable

questions.rationale: Ongoing assessment and family communication are essential. A sleeping or quiet infant may actually be unwell and must not be assumed stable.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: The infant becomes more responsive, feeds better, colour/perfusion improve, and temperature stabilises
Mottling worsens and feeding declines further
Monitoring is stopped after one observation set

questions.rationale: Improvement in young infants is shown by better responsiveness, feeding, perfusion, and temperature control.

cases.title: Anaphylaxis in a Child
cases.stem: A 7-year-old child, Maya, receives an antibiotic and within minutes develops widespread urticaria, facial swelling, coughing, and audible wheeze. She says her throat feels “funny” and then becomes frightened when she notices difficulty breathing. Her parent reports she had a mild rash with a medicine years ago but nothing this severe. The nurse notes rapid breathing, flushing, swelling around the lips, and increasing respiratory distress. The nurse recognises probable anaphylaxis.

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
questions.rationale: All findings fit anaphylaxis. The rapid progression after exposure plus airway and skin involvement is especially important.

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Systemic allergic reaction with airway compromise risk

questions.rationale: This is not a mild rash. The airway symptoms and rapid progression indicate an emergency.

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for airway obstruction and cardiovascular collapse from anaphylaxis

questions.rationale: Airway and circulation are the major threats in anaphylaxis.

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Activate emergency response and prepare immediate anaphylaxis treatment according to protocol while supporting airway and oxygenation
Delay action until the rash is measured
Ask the child to walk around to calm down

questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis requires immediate treatment. Delay can quickly become life-threatening.

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor airway, breathing, circulation, and response to treatment continuously
Reassure the child and caregiver with brief direct explanations
Document the suspected medication allergy clearly
Prepare for worsening airway obstruction if treatment is delayed or inadequate
Assume urticaria is the only relevant symptom

questions.rationale: All listed actions are appropriate except the false assumption that only the skin symptoms matter. Airway risk is central.

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Wheeze decreases, swelling lessens, breathing becomes easier, and the child appears less distressed
Respiratory effort worsens and voice becomes weaker
Monitoring stops because hives improve a little
The child becomes more cyanotic without escalation

questions.rationale: Improvement is reflected in easier breathing and reduction of airway and skin symptoms after emergency treatment.
